title: Skiing Near Seoul Without a Car: Jisan Forest Resort vs. Konjiam Resort
html:
If you want to try skiing or snowboarding in Korea but don't want to book an overnight stay in Gangwon-do, there's an easier option: two full-size ski resorts sit right inside Gyeonggi-do, the province that surrounds Seoul. Jisan Forest Resort and Konjiam Resort are both close enough for a single day trip (or a quick one-night stay if you want more slope time), and both are used often by first-timers who've never skied before. This guide covers what each resort is like, exactly how to book your lift ticket, and how to rent skis, a snowboard, or a full winter outfit if you didn't bring your own.

Jisan Forest Resort (Icheon)


Jisan Forest Resort in Icheon, Gyeonggi-do. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Jisan Forest Resort is in Icheon, about an hour from central Seoul by car or shuttle bus. It opened in 1996 and is one of the smaller, more beginner-friendly resorts near the city — it has 10 slopes, with gradients from a gentle 7 degrees up to a steeper 30 degrees, plus a dedicated sledding area and a zone just for small children. A moving walkway on the beginner slope carries you back up without a lift, which makes it one of the easiest resorts to try skiing for the very first time. The resort usually runs from around mid-December to early March, with slopes open from 9:00 AM until as late as 2:00 AM for night skiing (there's a short break from 5:00–6:30 PM for grooming), though exact opening and closing dates shift slightly each season depending on snowfall.

Konjiam Resort (Gwangju)


Konjiam Resort in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do — one of the biggest ski resorts near Seoul. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Konjiam Resort, in Gwangju-si, is often described as the largest ski resort in the Seoul metro area and is famous for being only about 40 minutes from Gangnam by car. It has nine slopes (four of them certified by the International Ski Federation for competitions) and an especially wide, gentle run that's popular with beginners and casual skiers, plus a separate condo and spa complex if you want to turn it into an overnight trip. For the 2025/26 season, Konjiam has been opening earlier than most other resorts — around 7:00 AM on weekends and holidays, 8:00 AM on weekdays — and also limits how many people are allowed on each slope at once, which in practice means shorter lift lines than you'd expect at a resort this close to Seoul.

How to Book Your Lift Ticket


A lift line at Jisan Forest Resort. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Both resorts sell lift tickets through their own official websites and apps (jisanresort.co.kr and konjiamresort.co.kr), but both sites are mostly in Korean, so first-time foreign visitors often find it easier to book through an English-language travel platform instead. Services like Trazy, Klook, and Pelago sell combo packages — lift ticket, equipment rental, and sometimes a round-trip shuttle bus from Seoul, all bundled into one reservation you can pay for in English before you leave your hotel. Some of these packages are explicitly listed as "foreigners only" and will ask you to show your passport at pickup or check-in to confirm you qualify — so bring it with you on the day.

If you'd rather book directly, Konjiam's app now handles the whole process — reservation, payment, equipment rental, and gate entry — in one place, which cuts down on ticket-counter waiting even if the app interface is in Korean (a translation app or browser pointed at your phone screen works fine for this). Whichever way you book, double-check this season's opening dates, operating hours, and ticket prices on the resort's own site before you go, since both can shift slightly year to year.

Renting Ski or Snowboard Gear and Clothing


Konjiam Resort's resort complex, where the main rental shop is located. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

You do not need to own anything to ski in Korea for the first time — both resorts have a rental shop right at the base of the slopes that rents skis or a snowboard, boots, a helmet, and poles as a set, and separately rents full snow clothing (padded jacket, pants, and gloves) if you didn't bring warm, waterproof layers. The usual process is: show up at the rental counter (or the pickup point, if you booked a combo package online), tell the staff your height and shoe size, try on boots and adjust bindings on the spot, and you're ready to head to the slope — the whole thing takes about 10–15 minutes outside of busy weekend mornings.

Renting equipment and clothing separately through the resort's own counter works fine if you're comfortable paying in Korean won on-site, but booking the rental as part of an online lift-ticket package (through Trazy, Klook, etc.) usually means you've already paid in advance and just need to show a booking confirmation, which can save time and confusion with language. Either way, goggles and gloves are sometimes charged separately or excluded from "equipment" bundles, so check exactly what's included before you book if you want to avoid a surprise extra fee at the counter.

Getting There Without a Car


Jisan Forest Resort's base area, where shuttle buses drop visitors off. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Neither resort is directly on a subway line, so the easiest option without a car is a round-trip shuttle bus from Seoul, which several tour platforms sell bundled with a lift ticket (and often equipment rental too) as a single same-day package — you get picked up near a major subway station in the morning and dropped back off in Seoul in the evening. Jisan Forest Resort has historically run its own network of free shuttle routes around the city in addition to these paid tour packages, though exact routes and schedules change by season, so confirm current pickup points directly with the resort or your tour platform before you go. A taxi is also an option for either resort if you're traveling in a small group and want to split the fare, but it's considerably more expensive than a shuttle seat.

💡 How locals actually do it: Many Korean skiers skip ticket counters entirely by booking everything — lift pass, rental, and sometimes a discounted early-morning or late-night session — through the resort's own app a day or two ahead, since online prices are often cheaper than walk-up prices and it avoids weekend queues.

Here's how the two resorts compare at a glance:

ResortLocationDistance from SeoulSlopesBest for
Jisan Forest ResortIcheon, Gyeonggi-do~1 hour10 slopes, moving walkway for beginners, kids' zoneFirst-timers and families
Konjiam ResortGwangju-si, Gyeonggi-do~40 minutes from Gangnam9 slopes (4 FIS-certified), wide beginner runShortest trip from Seoul, bigger resort feel

⛷️ Thinking about which one to pick for your first time on snow? Ask away in the comments — happy to help you plan it out!
